evals.query: I'm brand new to Kora and to compile-time DI frameworks. Teach me from scratch.
expected_behavior: Asks whether the learner is on Java or Kotlin, and whether they are coming from Kora 1.x, before choosing a starting point
Checks the environment first: JDK 25 or newer on the PATH and running Gradle, Gradle 9.x wrapper

Grounds the session on the Kora 2.0 refs (framework source at tag 2.0.0.RC2 and kora-examples at branch migration/2.0, plus the 2.0 docs) per R0, or says explicitly that it could not and is therefore teaching unverified
Starts from the smallest runnable service - the getting-started guide app - rather than an arbitrary topic
Teaches @KoraApp on an interface, the generated ApplicationGraph named after that interface, KoraApplication.run(ApplicationGraph::graph), and constructor-only injection
Has the learner compile with ./gradlew clean classes and open build/generated to see what was generated
Does not teach Kora through Spring/Micronaut/Quarkus analogies and does not invent behaviour
anti_behavior: Points the learner at kora-projects.github.io/kora-docs or a docs/v1 page as the source of Kora 2.0 answers
Uses ru.tinkoff.kora imports, the kora-parent BOM, or a 1.x version
States Java 21 (or anything below 25) is enough for a Kora 2.0 project

evals.query: Where's the official Kora 2.0 documentation? Just give me the link so I can read it myself this weekend.
expected_behavior: Gives https://koraframework.io/v2/en/ (or /v2/ru/) as the Kora 2.0 documentation, built from kora-docs branch feature/kora-2.0 mkdocs/docs/v2
Says the 2.0 docs are good reading but can trail the framework, so keys, defaults and signatures a lesson relies on are checked in the framework source (tag 2.0.0.RC2) before being relied on
Also points at the migrated examples at kora-examples branch migration/2.0 as runnable companions
Warns that the 1.x site kora-projects.github.io/kora-docs and docs/v1 pages describe ru.tinkoff.kora and are not a 2.0 answer
Warns that the per-app README prose in the migrated examples still links to the 1.x site, so the code and build files are the thing to read
anti_behavior: Hands over kora-projects.github.io/kora-docs as the Kora 2.0 documentation
Claims Kora 2.0 has no documentation site, or that docs/v2 is a copy of the 1.x pages
Presents the 2.0 docs as the final authority over the framework source

evals.query: I'm learning Kora with Kotlin. Show me the idiomatic way to write a repository method and a controller handler that calls it - I assume everything should be suspend and I should wrap the DB call in Dispatchers.IO?
expected_behavior: Corrects the premise: Kora 2.0 contracts are synchronous, executed on virtual threads, so a plain non-suspending function is the idiomatic form
States that suspend repositories, controllers and HTTP clients are not Kora 2.0 contracts at all
Explains that wrapping a Kora call in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) is pointless overhead on a virtual thread
Shows a plain blocking Kotlin repository method and controller handler with io.koraframework imports
If parallel fan-out comes up, points at Java StructuredTaskScope and states the rule of using the preview iteration of the chosen latest GA JDK rather than a copied signature
anti_behavior: Writes suspend fun on a @Repository, @HttpController or @HttpClient method
Recommends withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or runBlocking around Kora calls
Presents Mono/Flux or CompletionStage as a Kora 2.0 return type
Presents a StructuredTaskScope signature as fixed without naming the JDK it belongs to

evals.query: In my old Kora service I carried a correlation id and the tenant through Kora's Context so every layer could read it. Teach me how to do that in Kora 2.0.
expected_behavior: States that Kora's Context no longer exists anywhere in the framework - removed, not moved or renamed
Says the pattern must be redesigned rather than mechanically ported
Recommends passing the value explicitly as a parameter as the default answer, and explains why that is cheap on virtual threads and fits the compile-time model

Names JDK ScopedValue as the primitive that replaced Context inside the framework, citing io.koraframework.common.Principal (ScopedValue<Principal> VALUE, Principal.current(), Principal.with(...)) and the same idiom for MDC and telemetry

States the ScopedValue lifetime: the binding lasts exactly as long as the call it wraps (chain.process(request)), is visible on the request thread and on StructuredTaskScope forks inside that scope, and is not visible on an arbitrary executor

For genuinely ambient concerns, points at the mechanism that owns them - MDC via kora-aop-logging for log correlation, or an HttpServerInterceptor that sets and clears state around chain.process(request)
For an authenticated principal, points at HttpServerPrincipalExtractor and kora-http-server-auth rather than rebuilding a context object
anti_behavior: Shows an import of a Kora Context type in any package
Claims Context merely moved to io.koraframework.common or was renamed
Proposes a ThreadLocal holder as the lesson's answer without stating what it costs, or presents ThreadLocal rather than ScopedValue as the 2.0 replacement for ambient state
Claims a ScopedValue binding is visible to work submitted to an arbitrary executor

evals.query: My Kora 2.0 service builds green with ./gradlew clean build. That means it's correct, right? What else is there to check before I call this lesson done?
expected_behavior: Rejects the premise directly: in Kora 2.0 compilation is necessary but not sufficient

Names concrete silent failures - @Tag(HttpServerModule.class) on a global interceptor compiles but is never invoked; stale 1.x port keys are ignored without warning so the service listens on 8080/8085; telemetry metrics and logging are off by default; a tracing exporter with no endpoint exports nothing while tracing.enabled defaults to true
States that for anything on that list the acceptance criterion is a test or an observed response, never a successful build
Proposes a concrete exercise the learner can run, such as setting a stale port key and observing that the service answers on the default port instead
Points at @KoraAppTest / black-box testing as the tool for proving these
anti_behavior: Confirms that a green build means the service is correct
Lists only compile-time errors as the things that can go wrong
Claims stale port keys cause a loud 'Address already in use' failure as the normal symptom

evals.query: Explain how @KoraApp and Module interfaces build the application graph.
expected_behavior: Explains that @KoraApp goes on an interface whose extends clause names the modules the application is composed of
Names io.koraframework.common.annotation as the package for @KoraApp, @Component, @Module, @Root, @Tag
States that the graph class is generated at compile time and named after the interface (Application -> ApplicationGraph), and does not exist before the first ./gradlew classes
Explains the entry point KoraApplication.run(ApplicationGraph::graph), which takes a Supplier<ApplicationGraphDraw>
Explains that no reflection, classpath scanning or dynamic proxying is involved, and invites the learner to read build/generated to confirm
Points at a runnable companion app (getting-started guide app or kora-java-helloworld) and hands off to kora-di-compile for depth
anti_behavior: Puts @KoraApp on a class
Describes runtime component scanning or a runtime container
Uses ru.tinkoff.kora package names

evals.query: Walk me through building a first HTTP server endpoint in Kora, explaining every line.
expected_behavior: Follows the getting-started or http-server guide app rather than improvising a shape

Explains @Component, @HttpController and @HttpRoute as each is introduced, with correct packages: @HttpRoute/@Path/@Query from io.koraframework.http.common.annotation, @HttpController and the response types from io.koraframework.http.server.common.*
Shows a working return - HttpServerResponse.of(200, HttpBody.plaintext(...)) or a @Json record - and notes that UndertowPublicHttpServerModule must be in the @KoraApp extends clause
Has the learner run ./gradlew clean classes and look at the generated <Controller>Module
Suggests deliberately breaking it (removing the module from the extends clause) and reading the compile-time graph error together
Hands off to kora-http-server for anything beyond the lesson
anti_behavior: Returns Mono, Flux, CompletableFuture, or declares the handler suspend
Imports Spring or Jakarta REST annotations
Uses ru.tinkoff.kora imports or the 1.x UndertowHttpServerModule name without flagging it as 1.x

evals.query: Give me a 5-week plan for learning Kora with a runnable project at every step. I'm on Java.
expected_behavior: Lays out an ordered path starting with getting-started, then dependency injection, then config, then JSON/HTTP, then database and testing
Names real companion apps from kora-examples branch migration/2.0, using the actual directory shapes guides/java/kora-java-guide-<name>-app and examples/java/kora-java-<name>
Places testing early enough that the learner can prove the silent-failure cases, rather than at the very end
Notes which topics have no guide app (scheduling, SOAP) and points at the plain examples for those instead of inventing a guide app name
Offers to record progress in ~/.kora-teacher-progress.md and to read it back at the start of the next session
anti_behavior: Invents companion apps that do not exist, such as kora-java-guide-scheduling-app or kora-java-guide-di-app
Builds the plan around documentation pages (2.0 docs guides or 1.x kora-docs) instead of runnable companion apps
Includes removed integrations (R2DBC, Vert.x SQL, MinIO S3 client) as learning stops

evals.query: What do I need installed and what goes in build.gradle before my first Kora lesson?
expected_behavior: Requires JDK 25 or newer, and states that the JVM running Gradle itself must also be 25+ because io.koraframework:openapi-generator resolves on the buildscript classpath
Uses the platform "io.koraframework:kora-bom:$koraVersion" with koraVersion=2.0.0.RC2 from mavenCentral()
Java: annotationProcessor "io.koraframework:annotation-processors". Kotlin: ksp "io.koraframework:symbol-processors" with Kotlin 2.4.20 and KSP 2.3.12
Names Gradle 9.x (the framework pins the 9.8.0 wrapper)
Explains that Java 25 is a hard floor because the artifacts are class-file major version 69
anti_behavior: Uses ru.tinkoff.kora:kora-parent or any ru.tinkoff.kora coordinate
Pins 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT, 2.0.0.RC1 or 2.0.0.alpha6 for a new project
Says Kotlin learners can stay on JDK 21
Tells the learner to add --enable-preview as a blanket Kora requirement

evals.query: You keep saying Kora generates everything at compile time. Show me where to actually look.
expected_behavior: Names the output directories: build/generated/sources/annotationProcessor/ for Java and build/generated/ksp/ for Kotlin
Gives concrete generated names to look for - <App>Graph for @KoraApp, $Type_JsonReader / $Type_JsonWriter for @Json, $Repository_Impl for @Repository, <Controller>Module for @HttpController
Tells the learner to run ./gradlew clean classes first, because nothing exists before the processors run
States that generated code must never be edited as a fix - regenerate instead
Mentions that stale generated output is the cause of phantom ru.tinkoff.kora errors, fixed by clean plus --no-build-cache
anti_behavior: Suggests editing generated sources to fix a problem
Claims the wiring happens at runtime via reflection or a runtime container

evals.query: Teach me validation in Kora. I already know Bean Validation, so I'll just use the jakarta.validation annotations, right?
expected_behavior: Corrects the assumption: Kora validation is Kora's own, in io.koraframework.validation.common.annotation, and is not Jakarta Bean Validation / JSR-380
States that a jakarta.validation annotation is simply ignored by Kora - nothing in the framework reads it
Names real Kora constraints such as @NotBlank, @NotEmpty, @Pattern, @Range, @Size, @Min, @Max, @Positive, @Past, @Future, @OneOf, @Url, @UUID
Explains @Valid on a type (generates a Validator<T>) versus @Validate on a method
Points at the validation guide app as the runnable companion and hands off to kora-aop-validation
anti_behavior: Imports jakarta.validation.constraints.* as the way to validate in Kora
Calls Kora validation an implementation of JSR-380
Uses ru.tinkoff.kora.validation package names

evals.query: Next lesson: database. How do I run two writes in one transaction in Kora 2.0?
expected_behavior: Teaches executor().inTx(...) on the repository's JDBC executor as the way to run a transaction
States clearly that Kora 2.0 has no @Transaction annotation
Notes the config section is jdbc, not db, and names the symptom of getting it wrong (ConfigValueException at path ROOT.jdbc.username)
Mentions that repository contracts are synchronous - there is no reactive or suspend variant to reach for
For Kotlin, notes that inTx needs an explicit SAM constructor such as JdbcExecutor.SqlSupplier { ... }
Points at the database-jdbc guide app and hands off to kora-database-jdbc
anti_behavior: Introduces an @Transaction or @Transactional annotation
Uses getJdbcConnectionFactory() instead of executor()
Suggests R2DBC or a reactive transaction API

evals.query: I followed the observability lesson, hit /metrics, and I only see JVM metrics. Did I break something?
expected_behavior: Explains that component metrics and logging are disabled by default in Kora 2.0 while tracing is enabled, so nothing is broken
Shows enabling them per component, e.g. httpServer { telemetry.logging.enabled = true; telemetry.metrics.enabled = true }
Points at the observability guide app, whose own application.conf enables metrics explicitly for exactly this reason
Notes the system server exposes metrics and probes under httpServer.system with metricsPath / readinessPath / livenessPath
Uses this as a teaching moment for the wider rule that a green build proves nothing about telemetry
anti_behavior: Claims metrics are on by default and the learner must have misconfigured something
Uses the 1.x privateApiHttpMetricsPath key
Suggests adding a third-party metrics library instead of enabling the Kora telemetry switch

evals.query: Teach me global error handling for my Kora HTTP endpoints. In the project I copied from, the handler is tagged @Tag(HttpServerModule.class) but it never seems to run.
expected_behavior: Identifies the cause: 2.0 collects global interceptors by @Tag(HttpServer.class) from io.koraframework.http.server.common; HttpServerModule still exists so the 1.x tag compiles and is simply never looked up
Shows a correct handler: @Tag(HttpServer.class) @Component implementing HttpServerInterceptor with HttpServerResponse intercept(HttpServerRequest request, InterceptChain chain)
Uses this as the canonical example of a Kora 2.0 mistake that compiles cleanly and fails silently
Insists on a test that proves the interceptor fires, not just a successful build
Points at the http-server-advanced guide app and hands off to kora-http-server
anti_behavior: Leaves @Tag(HttpServerModule.class) in place or calls it merely deprecated
Claims the build would have failed if the tag were wrong
Uses @InterceptWith when the learner asked for a global interceptor, without explaining the difference

evals.query: We finished the DI and config lessons last week. Pick up where we left off, and by the way I now need to add real Kafka consumers to my actual service.
expected_behavior: Reads ~/.kora-teacher-progress.md to recover where the learner stopped, and updates it at the end of the session
Resumes at the next curriculum stop rather than restarting
Separates the two requests: continues teaching, and for the production Kafka work hands off to kora-kafka-consumer rather than improvising a lesson
Names the handoff explicitly so the learner learns the map of sub-skills too
Offers a project-local ./.kora-teacher-progress.md instead if the learner prefers, confirming it is git-ignored first
anti_behavior: Invents progress the learner never reported
Teaches production Kafka code from memory instead of routing to the domain sub-skill
Renames or relocates the progress file without saying so

evals.query: Skip the dependency injection stuff, it's boring. Just get me straight to writing REST endpoints.
expected_behavior: States concretely what they will hit without it - 'No component found for dependency' and 'Multiple components match' are the errors they will meet most often, and both are sentences about the graph
Offers the choice rather than refusing outright, with a short time estimate for the prerequisite
If the learner still wants to skip, proceeds with the HTTP stop and flags the DI concepts inline as they appear
Keeps the code correct regardless: @Component, constructor injection, correct io.koraframework packages
anti_behavior: Flatly refuses to continue until the learner does the prerequisite
Skips ahead silently without saying what was skipped or what it will cost
Drops correctness to move faster - field injection, invented annotations, or 1.x imports

evals.query: I've finished the basics. What else can Kora 2.0 do for a real service — I need scheduled jobs that run once per cluster, Postgres arrays and jsonb, rate limiting shared between replicas, and JSON logs without leaking tokens.
expected_behavior: Names the database-backed scheduler (scheduling-db-scheduler) for one-execution-per-cluster jobs and hands off to kora-aop-scheduling-db, contrasting it with the in-process JDK scheduler
Names the database-jdbc-postgres module (@Pg arrays and interval, PgRange, @PgJson/@PgJsonb) and hands off to kora-database-jdbc's postgres mappers reference
Names the Redis-backed distributed rate limiter / retry budget (resilient-kora-distributed-redis-lettuce) and hands off to kora-aop-resilient
Names Kora's built-in Logback JSON encoder and telemetry masking (DataMasker) and hands off to kora-telemetry-logging / kora-aop-logging
Says these topics have no guide app and are taught from the sub-skill and the framework tests
anti_behavior: Tells the learner to write a custom Logback JSON encoder
Suggests Quartz or the JDK scheduler with a hand-rolled database lock for one-per-cluster jobs without mentioning the db-scheduler module
Invents a guide app for these topics
